shortQuestions: The main theme is self-sacrifice and the power of hope. The will to live can save a person, and true art and love can give that hope — old Behrman sacrifices his life to paint a leaf that saves Johnsy.
Sue and Johnsy were young artists who met at a restaurant in Greenwich Village; they found that their tastes in art, food and fashion were so similar that they decided to share a studio apartment.

The doctor means that medicine alone cannot cure Johnsy; her recovery depends on her own will to live. Because she has lost hope and believes she will die, her chances are very poor unless she regains interest in life.
She kept asking Sue to open the curtains so that she could watch the ivy vine on the wall outside and count its falling leaves; she believed that she would die when the last leaf fell.

Her life was saved by the 'last leaf': old Behrman secretly painted a leaf on the wall during a stormy night. Seeing that the leaf did not fall, Johnsy regained hope and the will to live, and she recovered.

Seeing the last leaf still clinging to the vine after two stormy nights changed her views. She felt ashamed of her wish to die and said that something had made the leaf stay to show her how wicked she had been. We know it because she asked for soup, a mirror and said she hoped to paint the Bay of Naples one day.

Behrman was an old, unsuccessful painter who lived below the girls. He drank too much and was rough in manner, but he had a kind heart and was protective of the young artists. He always dreamed of painting a masterpiece; in the end he painted the last leaf on the wall in a cold storm, caught pneumonia and died — the leaf was his masterpiece.

Two young artists, Sue and Johnsy, share a studio. Johnsy falls ill with pneumonia and loses the will to live, believing she will die when the last ivy leaf falls. Sue tells old Behrman, who is moved. During a stormy night he paints a leaf on the wall. The leaf survives, Johnsy regains hope and recovers, but Behrman dies of pneumonia caught that night.
We learn that hope and the will to live are very powerful; we should never give up. The story also teaches selfless love and sacrifice — true greatness lies in helping others, as Behrman did.

Possible alternate ending: Behrman paints the leaf but is found the next morning shivering and ill. Sue and Johnsy, now recovering, look after him day and night until he too gets well. When the spring comes, the three artists exhibit Behrman's 'Last Leaf' and his long-awaited masterpiece is admired by everyone. (Any logical ending is accepted.)
activities: Sample summary — The Last Leaf: Beginning — Sue and Johnsy, two young artists, share a studio in Greenwich Village. In November pneumonia strikes and Johnsy falls seriously ill. Middle — She loses all hope and counts the leaves of an old ivy vine outside her window, convinced that she will die when the last leaf falls. Sue tells their neighbour Behrman, an old painter who has never painted his masterpiece. That night a cold storm blows, but in the morning one leaf still clings to the vine, and it stays the next day too. End — Johnsy feels ashamed of her despair, regains the will to live and recovers. Then Sue learns that Behrman has died of pneumonia: he had painted the last leaf on the wall in the storm — his true masterpiece.

Speaking activity guide: each student stands in turn and says three or four sincere compliments about the desk fellow, e.g., "Ali is always punctual", "He helps others in mathematics", "His handwriting is neat", "He is very polite". Only positive words are allowed; the class can note new adjectives of praise used.
